assessment.nobel_worthiness: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice idea and Ye's realisation of it turned atomic spectroscopy into the most precise measurement ever made, with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. This is quantum mechanics of atoms used to read out time and gravitational redshift at millimetre scales. It is clean, original and easy to explain, and it is the kind of fundamental, precision-driven result I value most.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength optical lattice and first demonstrated it with strontium. Ye's group brought the clocks to the 1e-18 level and linked them to frequency combs and to tests of fundamental physics. Two laureates give a natural and fair configuration. Hall and Hansch's earlier comb work does not interfere, but the committee would need to consider how Ye's wider contributions are described.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) have reproduced and improved the clocks. Their comparisons agree, and the field is moving toward a redefinition of the SI second. Recognition is timely and not premature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would treat optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize.
Yb, Al+ ion and other clock groups could press for credit, and I have not verified the full priority record.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms demonstrates the wave nature of massive particles and turns it into inertial sensors, measurements of G and of the fine-structure constant, and equivalence-principle tests. It addresses where the quantum world meets classical gravity, a question I find compelling. The impact on precision measurement is lasting.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group made the early atom interferometers, Bordé gave the theoretical framework and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, and Kasevich and Chu developed the light-pulse atom interferometer and its precision applications. Chu already shared the 1997 prize for cooling. The three credited names are reasonable, but Chu's omission and the overlap with other pioneers (Mlynek, Keith, Hänsch, Chu) leave attribution somewhat open.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in many laboratories over more than three decades, with commercial gravimeters and large-scale projects. The physics is stable and recognition could come at any time.
uncertainties: Fair division of credit among several early interferometer demonstrations (Mlynek, Pritchard, Chu, Kasevich).
Whether the committee prefers a discovery-type result to an instrument-type contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and E91 turned the no-cloning theorem and Bell-type nonlocality into a concrete information-theoretic security protocol. The idea is original and simple, and it links foundations to practice. It is closely tied to the 2022 prize on Bell tests, which strengthens its context without making it redundant.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard proposed BB84, and Ekert proposed the entanglement-based E91. Three people fit the prize limit. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea and the standing of the E91 versus BB84 contributions are points the committee must handle carefully.
assessment.maturity: Demonstrated over fibre and satellite links by several groups and used in commercial systems. Security proofs are mature, but practical implementations have known side-channel weaknesses. The physics is solid, while the real-world impact is still developing.
uncertainties: Whether the committee considers it physics or computer science and cryptography.
Priority of Wiesner's conjugate coding, which I recall from memory but did not verify here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model with tunable parameters. The Mott-insulator transition and quantum gas microscopy now allow direct observation of many-body states in a way that no solid-state system can. It is a clear case of an unexpectedly controllable quantum system leading to new insight into many-body physics.
assessment.attribution: Greiner (with Bloch and Hansch) saw the superfluid to Mott transition, Esslinger demonstrated fermionic Hubbard physics, and Bloch led the microscopy and wider programme. Zoller and Jaksch proposed the Hubbard-model realisation, so excluding the theorists is a real fairness problem. I choose the three experimentalists but flag that the theory credit is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced widely and still developing. The strongest results (Mott transition, spin and charge transport) are well established, but quantum simulation of open problems such as the 2D Hubbard model is still unfinished.
uncertainties: Zoller, Jaksch and Hansch credit versus the experimentalists.
Overlap with the BEC prize (2001) and with the other Zoller-linked quantum-computing candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping and cooling antihydrogen and comparing it with hydrogen, along with antiproton and proton magnetic moment measurements, test CPT symmetry at extremely high precision. It addresses a fundamental question about matter and antimatter, and it requires remarkable experimental skill in precision atomic physics.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse led the trapping of antiprotons and the ATRAP effort, Hangst led ALPHA to the trapping and spectroscopy of antihydrogen, and Ulmer (BASE) made the proton and antiproton magnetic-moment comparisons. The configuration is reasonable but the ATHENA, ATRAP and ALPHA collaborations share credit in a complex way.
assessment.maturity: Results agree with CPT so far, and ALPHA and BASE are improving precision. There is no unexpected discovery, and the field has only partial independent confirmation because few facilities can produce antihydrogen.
uncertainties: Only one facility (CERN AD/ELENA) provides these results, so independent confirmation is limited.
A null result for CPT, with no new physics so far, may reduce the case.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and the topological insulator concept gave a new classification of electronic phases based on topology and spin-orbit coupling. It is theoretically deep, experimentally confirmed and has influenced a whole field. It is outside my own speciality, so I defer partly to colleagues.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical proposal, and Molenkamp's group gave the HgTe experiment following Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang's prediction. Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu and Moore, and Konig and others are not in the credited list, so the credit is contested.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by several groups and techniques, including ARPES on Bi-based materials. The concept is stable and well established, although the 2016 prize recognised related topological phase work.
uncertainties: Significant credit disputes involving Bernevig, Zhang, Fu and Moore.
Overlap with the 2016 prize (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recollision (three-step) model and the quantum theory of HHG explain the plateau and cutoff and underpin attosecond science. I know this field well from my own work, and it is genuinely important. However, the 2023 prize already honoured the experimental HHG and attosecond pulse generation, so a further prize risks being seen as a repeat.
assessment.attribution: Corkum's semi-classical model and Schafer et al.'s work, together with Lewenstein's quantum-mechanical strong-field approximation, form the basis. The credited three are reasonable. I have collaborated with colleagues in this field and a recusal consideration may apply, so I rank it lower than I would otherwise.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and verified widely in many laboratories. The model is textbook, but the recognition may come after the 2023 prize and could be seen as already covered.
uncertainties: Whether the 2023 prize already covers the essential insight.
My own connections to the attosecond community may affect impartiality.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Inflation explains flatness, horizon and structure problems and predicts a nearly scale-invariant spectrum that has been confirmed by CMB data. The idea is of very high importance and originality. It is outside my expertise, so I defer to cosmologists, but I would not rank it higher without a decisive test.
assessment.attribution: Guth, Starobinsky and Linde are the usual core names, and Mukhanov, Albrecht, Steinhardt and Sato also have claims. The prize limit of three forces difficult choices, and I could not resolve the allocation.
assessment.maturity: The scalar spectrum is supported, but primordial gravitational waves have not been detected and alternatives persist. This is not yet a closed case, and recognition may be premature for a sceptical member.
uncertainties: No detection of primordial B-modes, so the specific inflationary mechanism is not tested.
Credit disputes involving Mukhanov, Sato, Albrecht and Steinhardt.
